title: The Best Classroom Management Strategy For A Crazy Class -crazy-class/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin addresses classes that are individually good kids but collectively silly, unfocused, and excitable, arguing the cause is almost always the teacher's own pace rather than the students themselves. His diagnosis is that moving, talking, and teaching too quickly injects tension that manifests as excitability. His three-step solution is to slow down: pause often and vary pause length to give students room to process and stay attentive; move with clear purpose, limiting unnecessary motion and standing still while giving directions; and proceed from one proven success to the next, only advancing once students demonstrate readiness rather than repeating instructions. He closes with the maxim 'slow is smooth and smooth is fast,' borrowed from military and first-responder culture, as the guiding principle for building a calm, focused class.
points: Diagnoses excitable, unpredictable classes as usually caused by the teacher's own excessive pace, not the students themselves.
Step one is pausing often, with varied pause lengths, to give students time to breathe, process, and refocus.
Step two is moving with purpose — limiting unnecessary motion and standing still during directions and independent work observation.
Step three is only advancing once students prove readiness, rather than repeating instructions or moving on prematurely.
Closes with the borrowed first-responder/military maxim 'slow is smooth and smooth is fast' as the guiding principle.
quotes: You’re going too fast. You’re moving, talking, and teaching at a rate that brings tension into your classroom.
Pausing also slows you down and reminds you to act, move, and speak with efficiency.
Teachers who rush around the room and bounce from one thing to the next always have excitable, ill-behaved students.
It means making sure they prove to you they understand and can do the work or perform the routine as taught.
The saying “slow is smooth and smooth is fast” is common among first responders and those in the military, but it’s also applicable to teaching.
By taking your time, moving deliberately, and doing things the right way, you limit mistakes, misunderstandings, and misbehavior.
